current_example.title: Example: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

q-140829.name: Question 1
q-140829.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{2}{3} & \,∗\, \\ 1 & 0 & \,∗\, \\ 0 & -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
q-140829.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the third column must be orthogonal to the first and second columns, and

- the norm of the third column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

q-93726.html:
Question 2
?

P=[2222∗00∗22−22∗] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[13−1313]
b
[22022]
c
[111]
d
[1−11]
e
[0−10]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 3×3 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the third column must be orthogonal to the first and second columns, and

  • the norm of the third column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [0−10] has both properties.
q-93726.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization

q-94253.name: Question 3
q-94253.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \,∗\, \\ 0 & 1 & \,∗\, \\ -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & 0 & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
q-94253.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the third column must be orthogonal to the first and second columns, and

- the norm of the third column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

q-94253.html:
Question 3
?

P=[120∗01∗−320∗] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[22−220]
b
[32012]
c
[3333−33]
d
[12032]
e
[−111]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 3×3 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the third column must be orthogonal to the first and second columns, and

  • the norm of the third column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [32012] has both properties.
q-94253.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization

q-94256.name: Question 4
q-94256.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \,∗\, & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \,∗\, & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 & \,∗\, & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
q-94256.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first and third columns, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

q-94256.html:
Question 4
?

P=[22∗2222∗−220∗0] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix P?

a
[022−22]
b
[−22022]
c
[00−1]
d
[010]
e
[−101]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 3×3 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the second column must be orthogonal to the first and third columns, and

  • the norm of the second column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [00−1] has both properties.
q-94256.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization

q-94252.name: Question 5
q-94252.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & \,∗\, & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & \,∗\, & 0 \\ 0 & \,∗\, & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
q-94252.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $3\times 3$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first and third columns, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

q-94252.html:
Question 5
?

P=[32∗012∗00∗1] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix P?

a
[−12320]
b
[−120]
c
[−111]
d
[01−1]
e
[12320]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 3×3 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 3×3 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the second column must be orthogonal to the first and third columns, and

  • the norm of the second column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [−12320] has both properties.
q-94252.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization

q-93727.name: Question 6
q-93727.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
q-93727.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=0.$ Computing $A-0I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{3}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 6
?

A=[−2111−2111−2],D=[−3000−30000] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[110]
b
[−22022]
c
[333333]
d
[3333−33]
e
[231323]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=−3, λ2=−3, and λ3=0. So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=0.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=0. Computing A−0I, we get

A−0I=[−2111−2111−2]−0[100010001]=[−2111−2111−2].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v3=[111],

where ‖v3‖=3. Dividing v3 by its norm, we obtain the third column of P: v3‖v3‖=13[111]=[333333]

q-94262.name: Question 7
q-94262.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
q-94262.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=0.$ Computing $A-0I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{6}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]
$$

q-94262.html:
Question 7
?

A=[123222321],D=[0000−20006] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix P?

a
[362336]
b
[66−6366]
c
[33−3333]
d
[16−2316]
e
[666366]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=0, λ2=−2, and λ3=6. So, the first column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ1=0.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=0. Computing A−0I, we get

A−0I=[123222321]−0[100010001]=[123222321].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v1=[1−21],

where ‖v1‖=6. Dividing v1 by its norm, we obtain the first column of P: v1‖v1‖=16[1−21]=[66−6366]

q-140837.name: Question 8
q-140837.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$
q-140837.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

q-94297.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
q-94297.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=0.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=0.$ Computing $A-0I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

q-94260.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
q-94260.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{6}.$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]
$$

q-94260.html:
Question 10
?

A=[1−10−121011],D=[000010003] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix P?

a
[333333]
b
[−132316]
c
[−22022]
d
[1−21]
e
[−666366]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=0, λ2=1, and λ3=3. So, the third column of P corresponds to the eigenvalue λ3=3.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ3=3. Computing A−3I, we get

A−3I=[1−10−121011]−3[100010001]=[−2−10−1−1101−2].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector

v3=[−121],

where ‖v3‖=6. Dividing v3 by its norm, we obtain the third column of P: v3‖v3‖=16[−121]=[−666366]
q-94260.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Distinct Eigenvalues

q-94351.name: Question 11
q-94351.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second and third columns of the matrix $P?$
q-94351.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the second and third columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{2}={v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{3}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{3} & ={v}_{3}-\frac{{v}_{3}\cdot {e}_{2}}{{e}_{2}\cdot {e}_{2}}{e}_{2} \\  & ={v}_{3}-\frac{1}{5}{e}_{2} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{2}$ and ${e}_{3}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the second and third columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ 0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{3}}{‖{e}_{3}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{24}{5}}}[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{30}}{15} \\ \frac{\sqrt{30}}{6} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{30}}{30}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-94351.html:
Question 11
?

A=[−12222−12−12],D=[−300030003] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second and third columns of the matrix P?

a
 [550255] and [010]
b
 [−10−2] and [211]
c
 [550255] and [55306−525]
d
 [−330−33] and [36306−36]
e
 [550255] and [3015306−3030]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=−3, λ2=3, and λ3=3. So, the second and third columns of P correspond to the eigenvalue λ2=3.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ2=λ3=3. Computing A−3I, we get

A−3I=[−12222−12−12]−3[100010001]=[−4222−1−12−1−1].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v2=[102] and v3=[120]

Notice that eigenvectors v2 and v3 are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set e2=v2=[102], and we find e3 as follows:

e3=v3−v3⋅e2e2⋅e2e2=v3−15e2=[120]−15[102]=[452−25]

Finally, dividing e2 and e3 by their respective norms, we obtain the second and third columns of P:

e2‖e2‖=15[102]=[550255]e3‖e3‖=1245[452−25]=[3015306−3030]

q-94332.name: Question 12
q-94332.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
q-94332.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=9.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are orthogonal. Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-94332.html:
Question 12
?

A=[40005−20−28],D=[400040009] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[−3300] and [333333]
b
[2200] and [001]
c
[100] and [0−2222]
d
[100] and [025555]
e
[−100] and [011]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=λ2=4, and λ3=9. So, the first and second columns of P correspond to the eigenvalues λ1 and λ2.

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to λ1=λ2=4. Computing A−4I, we get

A−4I=[40005−20−28]−4[100010001]=[00001−20−24].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[100] and v2=[021]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are orthogonal. Finally, dividing v1 and v2 by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of P:

v1‖v1‖=11[100]=[100]v2‖v2‖=15[021]=[025555]

q-140843.name: Question 13
q-140843.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second and third columns of the matrix $P?$
q-140843.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=4.$ So, the second and third columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{2}$ and ${\lambda }_{3}.$ 

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are  orthogonal. So, we divide ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ by their respective norms to obtain the second and third columns of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-140843.html:
Question 13
?

A=[301040103],D=[200040004] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second and third columns of the matrix P?

a
[−22022] and [010]
b
[−220−22] and [020]
c
[22022] and [010]
d
[12012] and [0−10]
e
[23130] and [001]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently, D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=2, λ2=4, and λ3=4. So, the second and third columns of P correspond to the eigenvalues λ2 and λ3.

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to λ2=λ3=4. Computing A−4I, we get

A−4I=[301040103]−4[100010001]=[−10100010−1].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−4I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[101] and v2=[010]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are orthogonal. So, we divide v1 and v2 by their respective norms to obtain the second and third columns of P:
v1‖v1‖=12[101]=[22022]v2‖v2‖=[010]
q-140843.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

q-94346.name: Question 14
q-94346.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
q-94346.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=7.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

A=[322232223],D=[100010007] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[−22022] and [010]
b
[−22022] and [−6663−66]
c
[220−22] and [−6366−66]
d
[−101] and [−12−1]
e
[10−1] and [22220]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=1, λ2=1, and λ3=7. So, the first and second columns of P correspond to the eigenvalue λ1=1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=λ2=1. Computing A−I, we get

A−I=[322232223]−[100010001]=[222222222].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[−101] and v2=[−110]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set e1=v1=[−101], and we find e2 as follows:

e2=v2−v2⋅e1e1⋅e1e1=v2−12e1=[−110]−12[−101]=[−121−12]

Finally, dividing e1 and e2 by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of P:

e1‖e1‖=12[−101]=[−22022]e2‖e2‖=132[−121−12]=[−6663−66]
q-94346.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 3x3 Matrix With Repeated Eigenvalues

q-94345.name: Question 15
q-94345.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
q-94345.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=8.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

Notice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set 

$$
{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\frac{{v}_{2}\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\  & ={v}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}_{1}}{‖{e}_{1}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ \frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{9}{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

A=[324202423],D=[−1000−10008] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that D=PTAP, where P is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix P?

a
[−22022] and [−26223−26]
b
[−13023] and [−26223−26]
c
[10−1] and [020]
d
[220−22] and [−3333−63]
e
[−22022] and [010]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

D=PTAP.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that A is symmetric and D is diagonal. Therefore, D=PTAP gives an orthogonal diagonalization of A.

From the diagonal matrix D we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are λ1=−1, λ2=−1, and λ3=8. So, the first and second columns of P correspond to the eigenvalue λ1=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to λ1=λ2=−1. Computing A−(−1)I, we get

A−(−1)I=[324202423]+[100010001]=[424212424].

Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives two eigenvectors:

v1=[−101] and v2=[−120]

Notice that eigenvectors v1 and v2 are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set e1=v1=[−101], and we find e2 as follows:

e2=v2−v2⋅e1e1⋅e1e1=v2−12e1=[−120]−12[−101]=[−122−12]

Finally, dividing e1 and e2 by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of P:

e1‖e1‖=12[−101]=[−22022]e2‖e2‖=192[−122−12]=[−26223−26]
